state.case_summary:
A 37-year-old African American woman with a history of hypertension, not on medication, who moved to the USA from Jamaica 5 years ago, presented with a persistent dry cough, intermittent low-grade fever, night sweats, fatigue, weakness, and exertional shortness of breath for 6 weeks. She reported no orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exposure to toxic gas or organic dust, weight loss, appetite loss, fever, or joint pain. She was a non-smoker and social drinker. On admission, her temperature was 100.2°F, pulse 113 beats/min, respirations 18 breaths/min, and blood pressure 150/80 mm Hg. The partial pressure of oxygen was 60 mm Hg on room air. The rest of her physical examination was normal. Laboratory data revealed a white cell count of 11,600 cells/μL with 82% granulocytes and 13% lymphocytes, hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume of 82 femtoliters, platelet count of 518,000 cells/μL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 117 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein of 7 mg/dl. A chest radiograph showed nodular infiltrates in the bilateral upper lobes of the lungs and peri-hilar fullness. A CT scan revealed extensive bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with areas of perihilar and peripheral consolidation. Pulmonary function tests indicated a mild restrictive pattern. The patient did not respond to an antibiotic regimen of erythromycin and ceftriaxone, which was later changed to moxifloxacin. Initial and repeated blood and sputum cultures for bacteria, mycobacterium, and fungus were negative. PPD and HIV ELISA tests were negative. Analyses for rheumatoid factor, anti-nuclear antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were negative. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was negative. A mediastinal lymph node biopsy showed only reactive anthracosis with no evidence of granuloma or malignant cells.

An open lung biopsy showed sharply demarcated patchy fibrosed areas with fibrotic plugs and lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, neutrophils and foamy macrophages.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
